C001.subject: Composite indices like HDI and GPI that incorporate community-level indicators
C001.object: the wellbeing of individuals in collectivist cultures
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Composite indices like HDI and GPI that incorporate community-level indicators the wellbeing of individuals in collectivist cultures]

qualifier.tension: Collectivist cultures prioritize relational harmony and community interdependence, yet global indices often weight individual achievements (income, education, health) more heavily. Empirical evidence is mixed: some studies show subjective well-being is higher in collectivist contexts despite lower index scores, while others argue that community-level indicators (e.g., social cohesion) are already partially captured, reducing the alleged bias. The direction and magnitude of any systematic underestimation remain contested.

C005.subject: Composite indices like HDI and GPI that incorporate community-level indicators
C005.object: the subjective well-being of individuals in individualist cultures
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Composite indices like HDI and GPI that incorporate community-level indicators the subjective well-being of individuals in individualist cultures]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-national survey data comparing HDI/GPI scores with individual life satisfaction ratings (e.g., World Values Survey, Gallup World Poll) across individualist vs. collectivist cultures, controlling for income and health. — Directly tests whether composite indices systematically overpredict subjective well-being in individualist cultures by correlating index components with self-reported well-being.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or quasi-experimental studies that manipulate the weighting of community-level indicators (e.g., social support, community participation) in well-being indices and measure changes in alignment with individual satisfaction in individualist samples. — Isolates the effect of community indicators on index scores versus individual subjective well-being, providing causal evidence for the hypothesized overestimation.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical reviews on cultural differences in the determinants of subjective well-being (e.g., Markus & Kitayama, Diener et al.) that critique composite indices for assuming universal relevance of relational factors. — Provides conceptual grounding for why community-level indicators may be less central to individualist well-being, supporting the hypothesis and guiding empirical tests.

qualifier.tension: These indices' inclusion of community-level indicators may artificially inflate well-being scores for individualist cultures by weighting relational factors that are less central to personal satisfaction in those contexts.

C006.subject: Composite indices like HDI and GPI that incorporate community-level indicators
C006.object: the subjective well-being of individuals in collectivist cultures
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Composite indices like HDI and GPI that incorporate community-level indicators the subjective well-being of individuals in collectivist cultures]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-cultural validation studies comparing HDI/GPI scores with individual-level life satisfaction surveys (e.g., World Values Survey, Gallup) in East Asian and Latin American collectivist societies — Directly tests the correlation between composite indices and subjective well-being measures in the specified cultural contexts, providing quantitative evidence for or against the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Ethnographic or qualitative studies examining how community-level indicators (e.g., social capital, inequality) in HDI/GPI align with local conceptions of well-being in collectivist cultures — Addresses the construct validity of composite indices by exploring whether their components capture culturally relevant dimensions of well-being, offering explanatory depth beyond correlation.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on the relationship between objective composite indices and subjective well-being in collectivist versus individualist societies — Synthesizes available evidence across multiple studies to identify systematic patterns, moderators, and gaps, helping to resolve the disputed status of the hypothesis with broader generalizability.

qualifier.geographic: East Asian and Latin American collectivist societies

C007.subject: Community-level indicators (e.g., social cohesion, trust) embedded in composite indices like HDI and GPI
C007.object: the well-being priorities of collectivist cultures relative to individualist cultures due to reliance on self-report scales that lack cross-cultural metric equivalence
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Community-level indicators (e.g., social cohesion, trust) embedded in composite indices like HDI and GPI the well-being priorities of collectivist cultures relative to individualist cultures due to reliance on self-report scales that lack cross-cultural metric equivalence]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-cultural validation studies of self-report scales used in indices like HDI and GPI, e.g., Schwartz's value surveys or World Values Survey items on trust and cohesion, comparing measurement invariance across individualist and collectivist societies — Systematic testing for metric and scalar invariance would reveal whether self-report scales systematically underweight collectivist well-being priorities, directly confirming or refuting the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Ethnographic or mixed-methods studies comparing composite index rankings (e.g., HDI, GPI) with community-validated well-being assessments in collectivist cultures (e.g., East Asia, Latin America, Africa) — If indices diverge systematically from locally derived well-being measures, this would support the claim of underweighting; convergence would refute it.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical literature on cross-cultural construct equivalence in well-being measurement, e.g., critiques of universalist assumptions in index design (e.g., work by Shweder, Kitayama, or Markus) — This can clarify whether the reliance on self-report scales inherently biases indices toward individualist priorities, providing a conceptual framework for interpreting empirical findings.

qualifier.temporal: since the widespread adoption of self-report scales in composite indices (post-1990)
qualifier.geographic: global, with particular relevance to comparisons between Western individualist societies and East Asian, Latin American, and African collectivist societies

C008.subject: Community-level indicators (e.g., social cohesion, trust) embedded in composite indices like HDI and GPI
C008.object: the distinct well-being priorities of collectivist cultures
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Community-level indicators (e.g., social cohesion, trust) embedded in composite indices like HDI and GPI the distinct well-being priorities of collectivist cultures]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-cultural validation studies of the Happy Planet Index and Human Development Index using data from the World Values Survey (e.g., Inglehart et al., 2014) — These studies can test whether the weights and components of HDI and GPI align with well-being priorities reported by collectivist populations in East Asia and Latin America, thereby confirming or refuting the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Qualitative comparative case studies of well-being indicator frameworks in collectivist societies (e.g., Bhutan's Gross National Happiness Index vs. HDI) — Analyzing how indigenous indices prioritize social cohesion and trust differently from HDI/GPI can reveal systematic omissions, providing evidence for whether composite indices fail to capture distinct cultural priorities.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of capability approach and cultural relativism in well-being measurement (e.g., Sen, 1999; Alkire, 2002) — This literature critiques universal indices for imposing individualistic values; applying it to HDI/GPI can clarify theoretical grounds for the hypothesis and suggest modifications to improve cultural sensitivity.

qualifier.geographic: East Asian and Latin American collectivist societies
